prize_parts.citation: For the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube observatory, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: The discoveries are at the centre, and B010 is a discovery in the plainest sense: a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice was turned into an instrument that found a diffuse flux of TeV-PeV astrophysical neutrinos, which nobody had seen before, and nature has since supplied clues in the form of the TXS 0506+056 blazar association, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane. The result has been confirmed through several independent channels and analyses, the interpretation of the flux as astrophysical is stable, and it tells us something about where cosmic rays are accelerated that no photon can. Three colleagues (Pearce, Olsson and I) placed it first or second, and the case does not rest on theoretical elegance but on observation. It is also timely: the window is open and calibrated, and waiting does not make the discovery any firmer.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. IceCube is a collaboration of hundreds, and the AMANDA lineage, the ice-calibration and optical-module work, and the analysis leaders (Yoshida among them) all matter, so any two- or three-name prize is a compromise that the committee would need expert advice to defend. The second reservation is maturity of the source physics: individual source associations are at only a few sigma, KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD do not yet offer comparable independent confirmation, and the origin of most of the diffuse flux is open. Finally, B010 has the thinnest broad support: Kroll and Lindroth both ranked it eighth, and if the committee values breadth of agreement, B043 is clearly ahead.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as a landmark of detector-driven discovery, favours the compact pair Halzen and Karle, and notes that source association is only at 3 to 4 sigma per object and that independent confirmation by KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD is not yet comparable.
responses.response: I agree with the pair and with the framing, and I think the caveat on individual sources is the right one, but it concerns the second chapter of the story, not the first. The diffuse flux is the discovery, and it is established by independent analyses within IceCube itself. The absence of a second telescope at comparable sensitivity is a real gap in the record, and I would still want the expert reports to address it before we sign off. I would also not lean on your point that neutrino detection was honoured in 2002: that prize was for solar and supernova neutrinos and cosmic X-ray sources, so neutrino astronomy at TeV-PeV energies is a distinct achievement.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B010 only eighth because attribution in a collaboration of hundreds is difficult, he says he can judge the instrument side better than the astrophysics, and he lists Yoshida as a third name alongside Halzen and Karle.
responses.response: The attribution difficulty is genuine and I do not dismiss it, but it is a difficulty the committee has handled before with instrument-and-discovery prizes, and it is not by itself a scientific objection. On Yoshida, I take the point seriously: he is credible, and I would like the experts to say whether his analysis leadership is on a par with Karle's construction role. I have kept the pair for now because the other candidates are also not free of attribution trouble. Your own top choice B043 asks us to omit Lemonde, Takamoto and the comb tradition, so a clean two-name outcome is not unique to it.

responses.point: Lindroth places optical lattice clocks first as basic atomic physics that is also precision science, with a clean Katori and Ye attribution, mature independent confirmation, and a natural place after the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing case and I move B043 up to my first alternative. I accept that it is mature, cleanly attributed and well confirmed, and that seven of eight members ranked it. My hesitation is not that it is wrong but that it is a refinement of precision time-keeping that the committee honoured in 2005 and 2012, and no new phenomenon was discovered. I would want to hear from you whether the redefinition of the second, which would give the prize a clear external anchor, is likely to precede or follow our decision, and I defer to you on the priority question between Katori and Ye's group.

responses.point: Olsson ranks lattice clocks first and IceCube second, and she calls the pulsar-timing result premature because it is at roughly 3 to 4 sigma with an unsettled origin and attribution spread over three collaborations.
responses.response: I ranked B021 second on the strength of its scientific interest and I concede your point. With significance short of discovery level, the Hellings-Downs signal still awaiting confirmation in combined data, and no natural three names, B021 is premature, and I withdraw it from my preferred configuration and from my alternatives. Your support of IceCube is welcome, and your request that the AMANDA to IceCube record be examined carefully is one I share.

uncertainties: How credit should be divided among Halzen, Karle, Yoshida and the AMANDA pioneers, which needs the outside expert reports.
Whether independent confirmation from KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD, or from improved IceCube source statistics, would change the case for or against waiting a year.
How much weight the committee should give to breadth of opening support, where B043 is clearly ahead, versus the discovery character of B010.
My knowledge of the IceCube record is from memory and I have not verified the details.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: my supervisor (Gross), mentor (Rubinstein) and co-author (Van Riet) are not credited on any shortlisted candidate. The profile does not say whether Uppsala colleagues take part in IceCube, which I would disclose to the committee if that is the case.
